interactive.title: Ride along one line
interactive.whatAmILookingAt: A short lesson in thirteen small screens on the squared grid from lesson 1, running 0 to 8 across and 0 to 14 up. Line 1, solid, is the equation that says what y equals, y = 2x + 1 on the first screens, rearranged to start "y =" first where it does not (y = 11 − 2x from 2x + y = 11), or saying what x equals on the last screen. Line 2, dashed, is the other equation. A point rides along line 1 only: slide it and it stays on the line, so its y is always line 1's rule worked out for its x. Beside the grid, line 2's equation is written with line 1's expression in place of y, such as x + (2x + 1) = 7, and drawn as two bars from a zero mark: one for the left side, worked out at the point's x, and one for the right side. A value below zero is drawn the other way from the zero mark. The bars match only when the point is on line 2 as well, at the crossing point, because that is the one point on line 1 that fits equation 2 too. The point clicks onto the crossing when it comes near, and the readout there gives the exact pair, such as (4/3, 11/3). Beneath the bars the working runs line by line: the swap, the like terms collected, x, x put back for y, and the check in both equations. When line 2 is parallel to line 1, the x's cancel, so the left bar stays the same wherever the point rides, at 1 for y = 2x + 1, and never matches the right one. When line 2 is line 1 written another way, the bars match everywhere. Some screens show an idea and the rest ask you to try it. A puzzle shows two equations and three answers. A wrong pick gets a one-line hint naming its slip, and Why? puts the pair into both equations.
interactive.ignores: The point rides line 1 only, but you could swap the other way, riding line 2 and putting its rule into equation 1, and the crossing comes out the same. Between clicks the readout rounds the point's x to tenths, but x can be any number. The grid shows a short piece of each line, which carries on both ways. The equations are example values, chosen so the working stays short.

explain.text:
When one equation tells you what y equals, you can write that in place of y in the other equation. That leaves one equation with one unknown,[^1] which you already know how to solve, and the first equation then gives y. Take lesson 1's pair, y = 2x + 1 and x + y = 7. Ride the point along line 1. Wherever it is, its y is 2x + 1, because that is the rule line 1 draws. So for that point, the x + y of equation 2 is x + (2x + 1). The two bars show that total beside 7, and they match only where the point reaches line 2, because that is the one point on line 1 that fits x + y = 7 as well. At the crossing point the y is the same in both equations, so the y in equation 2 is the very y line 1 gives, 2x + 1.

So write it in. Put the expression for y into the other equation,[^2] with a bracket round it: x + (2x + 1) = 7. Now only x is left. Collect like terms, 3x + 1 = 7, take 1 from both sides, 3x = 6, and x = 2. That is only half the pair, so put x = 2 back into y = 2x + 1 to get y = 5. Check in both: 2 × 2 + 1 = 5 and 2 + 5 = 7, so (2, 5) is the crossing point. Swapping an expression in for a letter like this is called [[substitution]]. It is exact, so lesson 1's crossing that fell between the tenths comes out too. With x + y = 5 you get 3x + 1 = 5, so x = 4/3 and y = 2 × 4/3 + 1 = 8/3 + 1 = 11/3, and 4/3 + 11/3 = 15/3 = 5.

When neither equation starts "y =", make y the subject of one first. Either equation would do; taking 2x from both sides of 2x + y = 11 gives y = 11 − 2x, and shows how to handle a minus in front of a bracket. Swapped into 3x − y = 9, it gives 3x − (11 − 2x) = 9. The minus takes away all of the bracket, so both signs inside change: 3x − 11 + 2x = 9. Then 5x = 20, x = 4 and y = 11 − 8 = 3. Check: 8 + 3 = 11 and 12 − 3 = 9. Change only the first sign, writing 3x − 11 − 2x = 9, and you get x = 20 and y = 11 − 40 = −29. The check in 3x − y = 9 gives 60 + 29 = 89, not 9, so checking in both catches the slip.

Sometimes the x's cancel. With y = 2x + 1 and y − 2x = 4, swapping in gives (2x + 1) − 2x = 4, which is 1 = 4. That is false whatever x is, so no pair fits both. The reason is that y − 2x = 4 is y = 2x + 4, with the same m as line 1 and a different c, so the lines are parallel, and there is no solution.[^3] On line 1, y − 2x is always 1, which is why the x's cancel. Ride the point and the left bar stays at 1, never reaching 4. With y − 2x = 1 instead, you get 1 = 1, true whatever x is, because line 2 is line 1 written another way, and there are endless solutions.[^4] Textbooks add that a pair of equations with no solution is called inconsistent,[^5] and the case of endless solutions is called redundancy.[^6] **Substitution puts what one equation says y equals into the other, which leaves one equation in one unknown;[^1] solve it, put the answer back for y, and check the pair in both.**

analogy.text: You know V = IR and P = VI. When you know the current and the resistance but not the voltage, you swap IR in for V and get P = (IR) × I, with V gone. Substitution does the same with a pair of equations. One says what y equals, so that expression can stand in for y in the other, and the letter it replaces drops out.
analogy.breaks: For a resistor that keeps its resistance, V = IR holds at every current, so P = (IR) × I is a new formula, true at every current. In a pair of equations, y = 2x + 1 holds only along line 1 and the other equation only along line 2, so when the lines cross once, the equation the swap makes is true for just one x, the crossing's.

practice.text:
- Pick the equation that says what y (or x) equals. If neither does, rearrange one, doing the same to both sides.
- Write that expression in place of the letter in the other equation, inside a bracket.
- Expand the bracket, minding a minus or a number in front of it, and solve for the one unknown left.
- Put that value back into the first equation to get the other unknown.
- Check the pair in both of the original equations.
- If the letter vanishes, read what is left. A false line such as 1 = 4 means no solution. A true line such as 1 = 1 means the equations are the same line, and every point on it is a solution.

**Rule of thumb:** Swap in with a bracket, and do not stop at x.

**Worked example:** y = 3x − 2 and 2x + y = 13. Swap in: 2x + (3x − 2) = 13. Collect like terms: 5x − 2 = 13, so 5x = 15 and x = 3. Put it back: y = 3 × 3 − 2 = 7. Check: 3 × 3 − 2 = 7 and 2 × 3 + 7 = 13, both true, so x = 3 and y = 7.

**Common mistakes**
- Changing only the first sign after a minus. 4x − (7 − 2x) is 4x − 7 + 2x, not 4x − 7 − 2x.
- Multiplying only the first term in the bracket. x + 2(x − 2) is x + 2x − 4, not x + 2x − 2.
- Rearranging with the wrong sign. 2x + y = 7 gives y = 7 − 2x, not y = 2x − 7.
- Stopping at x. The answer is a pair, so put x back for y.
- Checking in only one equation. (6, 1) fits x + 2y = 8, but not y = x − 2, as 6 − 2 = 4.
- Reading 1 = 1 as x = 1. No x is left, so it says every point on the line fits both.
- Taking the numbers in the equations as the answer. y = 3x + 2 and y = 3x − 4 have no solution, and (3, 2) fits neither: 3 × 3 + 2 = 11.

interactive.html:
A squared grid, 0 to 8 across and 0 to 14 up, with two straight lines and a point that rides along line 1. Beside it, two bars show equation 2 with line 1 swapped in. Every equation here is an example.

On the screens that show an idea, a faint ring marks the point you can drag. It moves in tenths along line 1 and clicks onto the crossing.
interactive.title: Ride along one line
interactive.brief: The one thing you should see is the bars for x + (2x + 1) and 7 matching only where the point riding line 1 reaches line 2, when you slide the point along line 1.

checks.label: When we solved a system by substitution, we started with two equations and two variables and reduced it to one equation with one variable: every swap here leaves one letter, and at every tenth along line 1 it gives the same total as equation 2 does for the point's own pair, which is what the left bar shows

Step 2, substitute the expression from Step 1 into the other equation: line 1's expression goes in place of its letter in equation 2, in a bracket when it has two terms, on every screen and in the first puzzle's answer

If the two lines cross, the coordinates of this intersection are the solutions to the simultaneous equations, and if the lines are parallel there is no solution: the bars match where the point reaches the crossing and nowhere else along line 1, the ring sits on both lines, and on the parallel screens the bars never match

When the two equations were really the same line, there were infinitely many solutions: on both same-line screens the bars match at every tenth along line 1, the working reads true whatever x is, and the puzzle takes endless solutions as its answer

Every puzzle's answers are checked against its own two equations: the right pair fits both and is the worked solution, every wrong pair misses at least one, a half answer is the right x or y alone, and every wrong answer has a hint of its own

Before an answer a puzzle keeps back the crossing ring and the solving, and the first puzzle its swap; a right answer or Why? draws them; a wrong pair on line 1 and on the grid sends the point there, where the bars do not match, and a wrong pair is put into both equations
The first screen shows only the swap and its value at the point; the solving lines arrive on the screens that solve, and only there
Dragging: the point stays on line 1, moves in tenths, stops at the grid's edge, and clicks onto the crossing when it comes near, where its label gives the exact pair (4/3, 11/3)

A value below zero is drawn the other way from the zero mark: at x = 0 on the make-y-the-subject screen the left side is −11, hanging below the mark, and on the no-solution puzzle the right side, −4, hangs below it while the left side, 2, stands above
Every demonstration finishes arriving within its 3 to 5 s, none starting before the 0.35 s screen fade ends, and a puzzle's drawing after an answer or Why? finishes within 2.5 s
